newsitem.title: USA: Alaska spill trustees nearing goal for land buys.
newsitem.headline: Alaska spill trustees nearing goal for land buys.

text.p: The panel administering the trust fund that settled environmental claims over the nation's worst oil spill has made a significant step toward its goal of shielding more than 640,000 coastline acres from logging and other development, officials said Thursday.

Late Wednesday, the Exxon Valdez Oil Spill Trustee Council solved a long-running dispute by striking a deal to buy or impose conservation easements on more than 75,000 acres in Prince William Sound, precluding large-scale logging there.
The council offered $45 million over five years for the Native-owned land, and the board of Eyak Corp., the group of Alaska Aleuts and Indians who own the land, agreed to the deal.
If approved by shareholders of the Native corporations, the Eyak purchase will add to 420,640 coastal acres already acquired by the council, officials said.

The council, made up of six state and federal representatives administering the $900 million civil settlement Exxon agreed to pay for natural resource damages from the 1989 disaster, has been seeking for years to protect the Eyak land from logging, a spokesman said Thursday.
"It's certainly one of the longest standing and most important efforts that the trustee council has worked on," said Eric Meyers, a spokesman for the council.
Some logging has already started on the Eyak land, Meyers said.
If approved by shareholders, the Eyak parcels will be combined with the Chugach National Forest and Alaska's Canoe Passage State Marine Park, the council said.

The council has used settlement money to acquire land in Prince William Sound, along the Kodiak Island archipelago and on the Kenai Peninsula. Those large parcels have been folded into existing state and national parks, national wildlife refuges and Chugach National Forest.
Still pending are planned purchases of more Native-owned lands along Prince William Sound and on Kodiak Island and Afognak Island, totaling 147,600 acres.
Habitat acquisition is considered an important method to help spill-impacted lands heal from the 11 million-gallon disaster, the worst in U.S. waters.

The Eyak land targeted for acquisition -- which includes 80 salmon streams, several lakes and lagoons, about 50 miles of freshwater shoreline and 150 miles of saltwater shoreline -- was a high priority because of its proximity to the grounding site and its importance to wildlife species damaged by the spill, officials said.
The council has also made some small land acquisitions, around the salmon-rich Kenai River and other sites.
